python-q1.testing: whether you know the GIL protects the interpreter, not your code, and can predict when threads help.
python-q1.trap: "the GIL makes Python single-threaded," or its opposite, "the GIL makes my code thread-safe."
python-q1.spoken:
"The GIL protects the interpreter's own state, not my data. In CPython every object carries a reference count that changes on almost every operation, plus shared structures like the allocator. The GIL is one lock per interpreter that makes those updates safe by letting only one thread execute Python bytecode at a time.

It stops mattering in two big cases. First, I/O: a thread releases the GIL while it waits on a socket or disk, so I/O-bound threads overlap fine. Twenty threads each sleeping 0.2 seconds finish in about 0.2 seconds. Second, C extensions: NumPy, PyTorch, tokenizers and most database drivers release the GIL while they do heavy work, so threads calling them can run in parallel. The real victim is CPU-bound pure-Python code: four threads doing Python arithmetic take about as long as one.

Two production consequences. The GIL doesn't make my code thread-safe: counter += 1 is several bytecodes, and a switch can land between them, so I still need locks. And one CPU-heavy thread in a web worker adds latency to every other request, because threads hand the GIL over only every 5 milliseconds by default.

Version note: Python 3.13 ships an optional free-threaded build without the GIL, and 3.12 allows one GIL per sub-interpreter."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.claim: it guards the interpreter, not your data
stages.html:
"The GIL makes CPython's internals safe to use from several threads. It says nothing about the safety of my own data structures."

  • CPython detail, not a language guarantee: PyPy has one too; Jython and IronPython never did; 3.13t can run without it.
  • One GIL per interpreter; a thread must hold it to execute Python bytecode.

stages.name: What CPython does
stages.claim: refcounts, a token, and a 5 ms hand-off
stages.html:
• Why it exists: every object has a reference count updated on nearly every operation; the allocator, dict resizes and list growth are shared too. One big lock made all of that safe without per-object locking, and kept single-threaded code fast.
  • When it changes hands:
    • a thread blocks on I/O (socket, file, time.sleep) → it releases the GIL;
    • a C extension releases it around heavy work (Py_BEGIN_ALLOW_THREADS);
    • otherwise the running thread is asked to drop it when another thread has waited for the switch interval (sys.getswitchinterval() → 0.005 s by default).
Work type Do threads run in parallel?
Waiting on network / disk ✅ waits overlap
NumPy / torch / hashlib on large buffers ✅ mostly, GIL released in C
Pure-Python loops, parsing, JSON in Python ❌ one thread at a time

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: scaling, and a race the GIL doesn't stop
stages.html:
"Run it and look at the shape: CPU-bound threads don't speed up, sleeping ones do."

import threading, time
def cpu():  sum(i * i for i in range(3_000_000))    # pure Python bytecode
def io():   time.sleep(0.5)                          # releases the GIL while waiting
def run(fn, k):
    ts = [threading.Thread(target=fn) for _ in range(k)]
    t = time.perf_counter(); [x.start() for x in ts]; [x.join() for x in ts]
    return time.perf_counter() - t
for fn in (cpu, io):
    print(fn.__name__, f"{run(fn, 1):.2f}s vs 4 threads {run(fn, 4):.2f}s")
# → expect: cpu ≈ 4× the single-thread time (no speedup); io ≈ the same 0.5 s (4× throughput)

And why the GIL isn't thread safety: += on a shared value is several bytecodes.

import dis
x = 0
def bump():
    global x
    x += 1
dis.dis(bump)
# → LOAD_GLOBAL x · LOAD_CONST 1 · BINARY_OP (+=) · STORE_GLOBAL x   (3.12; names vary by version)

A thread switch can land between the load and the store, losing an update. Use a threading.Lock, queue.Queue, or avoid shared mutable state.

stages.name: Where it bites in production
stages.html:
"The GIL rarely limits throughput of an I/O service. It hurts latency when CPU work sneaks into it."

Situation What happens Fix
FastAPI endpoint runs tokenisation / JSON-heavy parsing in a thread pool other requests wait on the GIL; p99 rises move CPU work to a ProcessPoolExecutor or a separate worker service
Background thread doing Python computation in a web worker convoy effect: I/O threads wake up and wait for the GIL offload to processes; keep web workers I/O-only
Embedding pipeline calling a model via torch fine with threads; the heavy work is in C/GPU threads or async are OK; watch data loading in Python
CPU-bound batch job threads give no speedup multiprocessing / process pool, or vectorise with NumPy
  • See it: py-spy dump --pid <pid> shows which thread holds the GIL and where; py-spy top for hot Python frames; asyncio debug mode for slow callbacks.

stages.name: What changes by version
stages.html:
• 3.12: per-interpreter GIL (PEP 684): sub-interpreters can run Python in parallel in one process (limited API).
  • 3.13: optional free-threaded build (PEP 703, python3.13t): no GIL, per-object locking and biased refcounting; single-threaded code runs somewhat slower, and C extensions must declare support.
  • Senior stance: not a default for production yet; adopt when your dependencies ship free-threaded wheels and you've measured a real gain for CPU-bound Python threads.

followUps.question: 🧪 Four threads each run for _ in range(1_000_000): x += 1 on a global. What does print(x) show?
followUps.html: Something up to 4,000,000, and you must not rely on it being exact. += is a read-modify-write across several bytecodes, so a switch between the load and the store loses an update. Recent CPython versions make lost updates rarer for this exact loop because of when switches are checked, but that's an implementation detail, not a guarantee. Protect it with a Lock.

followUps.question: "So Python can't do multithreading?"
followUps.html: It can, and does. Threads run concurrently and overlap all I/O; C extensions run in parallel with the GIL released. What threads can't do in standard CPython is execute Python bytecode on several cores at once. For that you use processes, or the 3.13 free-threaded build.

followUps.question: Why does one CPU-heavy thread slow down the I/O threads?
followUps.html: When an I/O thread's data arrives, it needs the GIL to run its Python code, but the CPU thread holds it. The waiting thread only gets it after the switch interval (default 5 ms) forces a hand-off, so every I/O wake-up can pay a few milliseconds. Many such waits show up as tail latency, the convoy effect.

followUps.question: Your FastAPI service's p99 doubled after adding a PDF-parsing step in a sync endpoint. What do you do?
followUps.html: Confirm with py-spy that parsing holds the GIL on the hot path. Then move it out of the web worker: a ProcessPoolExecutor via run_in_executor, or a separate worker service fed by a queue, so web workers stay I/O-only. Watch p99 and event-loop lag after the change, and size the process pool to cores.

followUps.question: Would you switch production to the free-threaded 3.13t build?
followUps.html: Not yet as a default. Check that every C extension you rely on ships free-threaded wheels, that your code doesn't rely on the GIL for implicit safety, and measure: single-threaded speed is lower, and gains only appear for CPU-bound Python threads. For most I/O-bound services the win is small today; I'd pilot it on a CPU-heavy batch job first.

followUps.question: Why do threads calling NumPy scale when pure-Python threads don't?
followUps.html: NumPy releases the GIL inside its C loops for large arrays, so several threads can compute at once on different cores. The Python lines between those calls still take the GIL, so small arrays with lots of Python overhead scale poorly.

dontSay: "The GIL makes Python single-threaded." — threads run and overlap I/O.
"The GIL makes my code thread-safe." — compound operations still race.
"Python is slow because of the GIL." — most slowness is interpretation overhead, not the lock.
"The GIL is part of the Python language." — it's a CPython implementation detail.

spine: What I'd pick for an AI backend
python-q2.testing: whether you choose by where the time goes, not by taste or fashion.
python-q2.trap: "asyncio is the modern one, so always asyncio," or "threads are useless because of the GIL."
python-q2.spoken:
"I pick by asking one question first: where does the time actually go? I measure that before choosing.

If the time is spent waiting on the network or disk, and my libraries are async, I use asyncio. One thread and one event loop can hold thousands of open sockets, because a coroutine gives up control at every await. That's the shape of an AI backend: most of a request is waiting on the model provider, the vector store or Postgres.

If it's waiting, but the library I need is sync-only, like an old SDK or boto3, I use a bounded thread pool. Threads release the GIL while they block on I/O, so they overlap fine; I just cap the pool so I don't spawn thousands.

If it's burning CPU in pure Python bytecode, like parsing or feature loops, threads won't help because of the GIL, so I use processes: a ProcessPoolExecutor or a separate worker service.

And if the CPU work is inside C, like NumPy, torch or tokenizers, the GIL is already released, so threads are fine and cheaper than processes.

In practice I mix them: an async API, to_thread for the odd sync call, and a process pool or worker tier for heavy CPU work."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.claim: waiting vs computing, and in which language
stages.html:
"The choice isn't about style. It's about whether the time is waiting or computing, and whether the computing is in Python or in C."

Where the time goes Tool Why
Waiting, async library available asyncio one thread, thousands of concurrent waits
Waiting, sync-only library thread pool threads release the GIL while blocked
CPU in Python bytecode processes each process has its own GIL
CPU in C (NumPy, torch) threads the extension releases the GIL
  • Measure first: wall-clock vs CPU time. time.perf_counter() vs time.process_time() on one request tells you which row you're in.

stages.name: Where asyncio wins
stages.html:
• A coroutine costs a few KB; a thread costs a stack (MBs of reserved virtual memory) plus OS scheduling.
  • Explicit await points make shared state easier to reason about: no switch can happen between two lines without an await.
  • Cost: everything on the path must be async. One blocking call stalls every request on that loop (see blocking-call-in-async-handler).

💻 Prove it — 100 concurrent waits on one thread:

import asyncio, time, threading
async def call():
    await asyncio.sleep(0.5)          # stands in for an HTTP call to a model provider
async def main():
    t = time.perf_counter()
    await asyncio.gather(*(call() for _ in range(100)))
    print(f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.1f}s", threading.active_count())
asyncio.run(main())
# → 0.5s 1   (100 waits overlap; one thread)

stages.name: Where threads win
stages.html:
• A thread blocked on a socket releases the GIL, so a pool of 20 threads makes 20 sync HTTP calls overlap.
  • NumPy, torch, hashlib and most tokenizers release the GIL inside C loops: threads get real parallelism there with shared memory and no pickling.
  • Cost: preemptive switching means data races on shared state (x += 1 is not atomic); unbounded pools exhaust memory and file descriptors.
  • From async code: await asyncio.to_thread(sync_fn, arg) (3.9+) runs it on the loop's default executor.

stages.name: Where processes win
stages.html:
• Each process has its own interpreter and its own GIL, so Python bytecode runs on several cores.
  • Cost: arguments and results are pickled across the boundary; each process pays startup and holds its own copy of anything it loads (a model loaded in 8 workers is 8 copies).
  • spawn vs fork changes startup and memory (see multiprocessing-linux-vs-mac).
  • Rule of thumb: worth it when each task does far more work than it costs to pickle its inputs.

stages.name: What I'd pick for an AI backend
stages.claim: all three, each in its lane
stages.html:
"Async at the edge, threads for sync stragglers, processes or a worker tier for Python CPU work."

  • Version note: 3.13's free-threaded build (python3.13t) makes threads viable for Python CPU work, but only once every C extension you use supports it.

followUps.question: 🧪 What does this print, and roughly how long does it take?  then
followUps.html: It prints nothing and takes about 3 seconds, not 1. time.sleep blocks the thread, and the loop can't switch to the next coroutine until f returns. The coroutines run one after another. await asyncio.sleep(1) would take about 1 second.

followUps.question: "Threads are useless in Python because of the GIL, right?"
followUps.html: No. Threads overlap any blocking I/O and run in parallel inside C extensions that release the GIL. What they can't do in standard CPython is run Python bytecode on two cores at once.

followUps.question: Why not just use asyncio for everything?
followUps.html: Because it only helps waiting, and only if every call on the path is async. A CPU loop inside a coroutine blocks the loop just like time.sleep. Sync-only SDKs need a thread anyway, and Python-heavy CPU work needs processes.

followUps.question: How big should the thread pool be for sync calls to an LLM provider?
followUps.html: Size it by concurrency, not cores: roughly target throughput × call latency (Little's law), capped by the provider's rate limit and by memory. 10 req/s × 2 s latency needs about 20 in flight. The default to_thread executor is min(32, cpu_count + 4) threads, so set your own when it matters.

followUps.question: Your FastAPI service does async calls plus a 300 ms pure-Python post-processing step. Design it.
followUps.html: Keep the provider calls async. Move the 300 ms step off the loop: a ProcessPoolExecutor via loop.run_in_executor if the inputs are small to pickle, or a queue to a worker service if it's spiky or needs its own scaling. Watch event-loop lag and p99 before and after; the win shows up as tail latency.

followUps.question: Does 3.13 free-threading change your answer?
followUps.html: For I/O-bound work, no: asyncio is still the right tool. For Python CPU work, it could let threads replace processes and avoid pickling, but only once every C extension ships free-threaded wheels and I've measured the single-thread slowdown. Today I'd pilot it on a batch job, not the API.

dontSay: "asyncio is always faster." — it's only better at waiting.
"Threads don't work in Python." — they do for I/O and C-heavy work.
"Use multiprocessing for I/O." — it pays process and pickling costs for nothing.
Choosing before measuring where the time goes.

spine: The production version of the trap
python-q3.testing: whether you can name definition-time evaluation, not just the symptom.
python-q3.trap: "Python keeps the list between calls" with no explanation of why.
python-q3.spoken:
"Default values are evaluated once, when the def statement runs, not each time the function is called. The resulting object is stored on the function object, in __defaults__. So if the default is a list or a dict, every call that doesn't pass that argument gets the same list, and any mutation leaks into the next call.

The classic symptom is a function like def add(item, bucket=[]) that returns [1], then [1, 2], then [1, 2, 3].

The fix is a sentinel: default to None, and build the new list inside the body. If None is a valid input, I use a private _MISSING = object() sentinel instead.

In a service it's worse than a quirk: the shared default lives as long as the worker process, so it becomes accidental global state, shared across requests and even across tenants."

stages.name: Predict it out loud
stages.html:
def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket
print(add(1)); print(add(2)); print(add(3, [])); print(add(4))
# → [1]
# → [1, 2]
# → [3]
# → [1, 2, 4]

"The third call passes its own list, so it's clean. The fourth goes back to the shared default."

stages.name: Trace it step by step
stages.claim: one object, stored on the function
stages.html:
• def runs → evaluates [] → stores it in add.__defaults__.
  • Each call without bucket binds the local name to that same object.
  • .append mutates it in place; rebinding (bucket = bucket + [x]) would not.

💻 Prove it:

def add(item, bucket=[]):
    bucket.append(item); return bucket
print(add.__defaults__)
add(1); add(2)
print(add.__defaults__)
print(add(9) is add.__defaults__[0])
# → ([],)
# → ([1, 2],)
# → True

stages.name: The rule that decides it
stages.html:
• Language guarantee: default expressions are evaluated once, left to right, when the function is defined.
  • Immutable defaults (0, None, "x", tuples) are safe because they can't be mutated.
  • Fix:
_MISSING = object()
def add(item, bucket=None):
    if bucket is None:
        bucket = []
    bucket.append(item)
    return bucket

stages.name: Variants that flip the answer
stages.html:
Variant Shared? Why
def f(ts=datetime.now()) yes, frozen timestamp evaluated once at import
class A: items = [] yes, across instances class attribute, mutated via self.items.append
@dataclass with items: list = [] error dataclasses reject it; use field(default_factory=list)
Pydantic field tags: list = [] no Pydantic copies defaults per instance
def f(x=None) then x = x or [] subtle bug an empty list passed in is replaced too

stages.name: The production version
stages.html:
• In a long-running FastAPI or Celery worker, a mutable default lives for the process lifetime: one request's data appears in another's.
  • A default headers={} that a helper mutates can leak an auth header between tenants.
  • Guard: ruff rule B006 (flake8-bugbear) flags mutable defaults; B008 flags function calls in defaults.

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints?  then
followUps.html: 1 2 2. The dict is shared, so it grows to two keys and the repeated 2 overwrites. This is also the "intentional" use: a mutable default as a poor man's memo cache. Prefer functools.lru_cache, which is explicit and bounded.

followUps.question: Why did Python choose def-time evaluation?
followUps.html: It's simple and fast: defaults are computed once instead of on every call, and the rule is the same for all expressions. Call-time defaults would need to capture and re-run arbitrary code each call. PEP 671 proposed late-bound defaults (=>) but wasn't accepted.

followUps.question: "So mutable defaults are always wrong?"
followUps.html: Almost always in application code. The exceptions are deliberate: a memo dict in a tiny script, or a default you never mutate. Even then, a None sentinel or an explicit cache is clearer to the next reader.

followUps.question: What's wrong with ?
followUps.html: An empty list passed by the caller is falsy, so it gets replaced with a new list and the caller's list is never filled. Use if bucket is None to test for "not passed".

followUps.question: Where have you seen this cause a real incident pattern?
followUps.html: The pattern is shared state leaking across requests in a long-lived worker: a default dict of headers or context mutated per request. It shows up as data from one user in another's response, only under load. The fix is the sentinel plus a lint rule in CI so it can't come back.

dontSay: "Python caches the list between calls." — it's one object created at def time.
"Defaults are evaluated each call." — they're not.
"Use x = x or []." — it breaks on empty inputs.

python-q4.testing: identity vs equality, and whether you know interning is a CPython detail.
python-q4.spoken:
"== asks whether two objects have equal values, by calling __eq__. is asks whether they are the same object, which in CPython means the same memory address. It can't be overridden.

is sometimes looks right by accident because CPython caches some objects. Small integers from −5 to 256 are preallocated, so a = 100; b = 100; a is b is true. Short identifier-like strings are often interned too. But that's a CPython implementation detail, not a language rule: a = 1000; b = 1000 may or may not be the same object, depending on whether they were created in the same code block.

So I use is only for singletons and sentinels: None, True/False in rare cases, enum members, and my own _MISSING = object(). For everything else I use ==. Linters flag is with a literal, and since 3.8 CPython itself warns with a SyntaxWarning."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"== compares values through __eq__; is compares identity and can't be overloaded."

  • a == b → type(a).__eq__(a, b), falls back to b.__eq__(a), then identity.
  • a is b → same object; id(a) == id(b) while both are alive.

stages.name: What CPython does
stages.claim: caches that make is pass by luck
stages.html:
• Small int cache (CPython detail): −5..256 are preallocated singletons.
  • String interning (CPython detail): identifier-like literals and names are interned at compile time; sys.intern() does it explicitly.
  • Constant folding: equal literals in the same code object may share one constant.
Expression Result Guaranteed?
x is None reliable yes, None is a singleton
256 is 256-style small ints usually True no, CPython detail
int("1000") is int("1000") False no
[] is [] False yes, two new lists

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
a = int("256"); b = int("256")
c = int("257"); d = int("257")
print(a is b, c is d, c == d)
s = "".join(["ab", "c"]); t = "abc"
print(s == t, s is t, __import__("sys").intern(s) is t)
# → True False True
# → True False True

int("…") builds the value at runtime, so constant folding can't help: 256 hits the cache, 257 doesn't.

stages.name: Where it bites in production
stages.html:
• Legit: if x is None, sentinel objects, enum members (status is Status.DONE), type(x) is dict for exact type checks.
  • Bug: if response.status_code is 200 passes in tests with small values cached and is a SyntaxWarning since 3.8; compare with ==.
  • Bug: NumPy/pandas: arr == 0 returns an array, so if arr == 0 raises "truth value is ambiguous"; is there is wrong too. Use .all()/.any() or np.array_equal.
  • Floats: == on floats needs tolerance: math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3).
  • NaN: float("nan") == float("nan") is False, but x is x is True, which is why [nan] == [nan] is True (containers check identity first).

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints?
followUps.html: True False. x == x compares the lists; list comparison checks identity before == for each element, and the NaN is the same object, so it counts as equal. x[0] == x[0] calls float equality directly, and NaN is never equal to itself.

followUps.question: "Is is faster than ==?"
followUps.html: Slightly, because it's a pointer compare with no method call. But speed isn't the reason to pick it: it answers a different question. Using it for values gives wrong answers that happen to pass on small inputs.

followUps.question: Why is x is None preferred over x == None?
followUps.html: None is a guaranteed singleton, so identity is exact. == calls __eq__, which a class can override to return anything, including a NumPy array. PEP 8 says compare singletons with is.

followUps.question: What's the contract between __eq__ and __hash__?
followUps.html: Objects that compare equal must have equal hashes. Defining __eq__ without __hash__ sets __hash__ to None, making instances unhashable. Mutable objects whose equality depends on mutable fields shouldn't be hashable, or they get lost in dicts after a change.

followUps.question: Where would you legitimately compare types with is?
followUps.html: Exact dispatch where subclasses must not match: type(x) is bool before int, because bool is a subclass of int, a real bug in JSON-schema generation and config parsing. Otherwise isinstance is right because it respects inheritance.

dontSay: "Small ints are always the same object." — CPython detail, not a rule.

python-q5.testing: that you know generators buy memory, not speed, and can build a streaming pipeline with them.
python-q5.spoken:
"A generator produces values on demand instead of building them all up front. When you call a generator function, nothing runs; you get a generator object that holds a suspended frame. Each next() runs the body until the next yield, hands back one value, and freezes the frame again, locals and all.

That gives constant memory regardless of how much data flows through. If I'm ingesting a million documents for embedding, I can chain read, parse, chunk, filter and batch as generators, and at any moment only the current item and the current batch are in memory. A list-based version would hold every stage's full output at once.

What it doesn't buy is speed. Per item, a generator is usually a bit slower than a list comprehension. And there are real costs: it's single-pass, so iterating it twice gives nothing the second time; there's no len(); and retrying from the middle of a failed pipeline is harder, so I checkpoint by document ID.

Generators are also the ancestor of coroutines: send() and yield from are how async was first built in Python."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"A generator trades a materialised list for a suspended frame: memory stays flat no matter how long the stream is."

  • Calling a generator function returns a generator object; the body hasn't started.
  • next() resumes until yield; StopIteration at the end, which for handles.

stages.name: What CPython does
stages.claim: a frame that survives between calls
stages.html:
• A normal function's frame is discarded on return; a generator keeps its frame (locals, instruction pointer, the evaluation stack) alive between next() calls.
  • The generator object itself is small and constant-size; the data it produces is created one item at a time.
  • yield from sub delegates to a sub-iterator, forwarding send()/throw() too.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
import sys
nums_list = [i * i for i in range(1_000_000)]
nums_gen  = (i * i for i in range(1_000_000))
print(sys.getsizeof(nums_list) > 8_000_000, sys.getsizeof(nums_gen) < 300)
g = (x for x in range(3))
print(list(g), list(g))
# → True True
# → [0, 1, 2] []

getsizeof on the list counts only its pointer array (8 bytes × 1M), not the int objects; the real gap is larger.

stages.name: Where it bites in production
stages.html:
def read(paths):
    for p in paths:
        with open(p) as f: yield f.read()
def chunk(docs, n):   yield from (d[i:i+n] for d in docs for i in range(0, len(d), n))
def batched(it, k):
    batch = []
    for x in it:
        batch.append(x)
        if len(batch) == k: yield batch; batch = []
    if batch: yield batch
for b in batched(chunk(read(paths), 1000), 64): embed(b)
Pitfall What happens Fix
Iterating twice second pass is empty materialise once, or re-create the generator
Failure mid-stream where did we stop? checkpoint IDs; make the sink idempotent
Open files inside a generator file stays open until exhausted or GC'd with inside the generator; close the generator
Exceptions raised at the consumer's next(), far from the cause log with item IDs in each stage
list(gen) "to debug" memory spike, defeats the point itertools.islice(gen, 5)
  • See it: tracemalloc peak with list vs generator versions; memray for the flame graph.

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints?  then
followUps.html: made, then start, then 1. Calling g() only creates the generator; the body runs at the first next().

followUps.question: "Generators are faster than lists, right?"
followUps.html: No. Per item they're usually a little slower because each value costs a frame resume. The win is memory, and sometimes latency to the first item. If the data fits comfortably and you iterate it several times, a list is simpler and faster.

followUps.question: Generator expression vs list comprehension — when each?
followUps.html: List comprehension when you need the result more than once, need len() or indexing, or it's small. Generator expression when it feeds straight into a consumer like sum(), any(), "".join() or a pipeline. any(x > 0 for x in xs) also short-circuits.

followUps.question: How do you make a generator pipeline resumable after a crash?
followUps.html: Give every item a stable ID, write a checkpoint after each committed batch, and make the sink idempotent (upsert by ID). On restart, skip IDs up to the checkpoint. The pipeline stays lazy; durability lives in the checkpoint, not the generator.

followUps.question: How do generators relate to async?
followUps.html: Both are suspendable frames. Before async def (3.5), asyncio coroutines were generators using yield from. Today coroutines are a separate type, and async generators (async def with yield) stream items from async sources, like tokens from an LLM.

followUps.question: What happens to a with open() inside a generator you stop consuming?
followUps.html: The file stays open until the generator is closed. close() raises GeneratorExit at the paused yield, which runs the with exit. In CPython that happens as soon as the last reference goes away; on other runtimes it may wait for GC. Close generators explicitly or wrap them in contextlib.closing.

dontSay: "A generator stores its values." — it stores a paused frame.

python-q6.testing: that hints aren't enforced, and that you know which libraries read them and why that matters for AI backends.
python-q6.spoken:
"By default, nothing. CPython evaluates annotations and stores them in __annotations__, and then ignores them. Passing a string to a function annotated int runs fine until the code does something a string can't.

The value is in tools that read them. Statically, mypy or pyright catch type errors before runtime, and the IDE uses them for completion and safe refactors. At runtime, some libraries read the annotations on purpose and act on them: dataclasses build __init__ from them, Pydantic validates and coerces data against them, and FastAPI uses them to parse requests and generate the OpenAPI schema.

That runtime reading is how LLM tool calling works in Python: a function signature or a Pydantic model becomes a JSON Schema that you send to the model as a tool definition.

One detail matters: with from __future__ import annotations, and by default from 3.14, annotations are stored lazily rather than evaluated at definition time. Code that reads them should use typing.get_type_hints() or, on 3.14, annotationlib, not __annotations__ directly."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"Annotations are metadata. The interpreter keeps them and never checks them."

  • Language guarantee: annotations don't affect execution (PEP 484 is about tools).
  • They live in func.__annotations__, Class.__annotations__, module __annotations__.

stages.name: What CPython does
stages.html:
Mode When annotations are evaluated What __annotations__ holds
default, ≤ 3.13 at def/class time the evaluated objects
from __future__ import annotations never, unless someone asks strings
3.14 default (PEP 649/749) lazily, on first access the evaluated objects, computed on demand
  • Forward references ("Node") resolve later via typing.get_type_hints().

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: ignored by the interpreter, used by a library
stages.html:
from dataclasses import dataclass
def double(x: int) -> int:
    return x * 2
print(double("ab"), double.__annotations__)
@dataclass
class Point:
    x: int
    y: int = 0
print(Point("oops"))
# → abab {'x': <class 'int'>, 'return': <class 'int'>}
# → Point(x='oops', y=0)

Dataclasses read the annotations to build __init__ but don't validate. Pydantic would raise a ValidationError for x="oops".

stages.name: Where it bites in production
stages.html:
• FastAPI: parameter annotations decide query vs body vs path, run Pydantic validation, and produce OpenAPI docs.
  • LLM tools: Model.model_json_schema() or a function signature → tool definition; the model's arguments come back and are validated against the same model.
  • Decorators: a wrapper without functools.wraps hides the original annotations, and FastAPI sees *args, **kwargs (see timing-decorator).
  • Hot paths: get_type_hints() is slow; libraries cache it. Don't call it per request.
  • CI: mypy --strict or pyright on the service; untyped boundaries are where bugs hide.

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints?  then  then
followUps.html: {'x': 'int'} — the annotation is stored as a string. typing.get_type_hints(f) resolves it to {'x': <class 'int'>}. Libraries that read raw __annotations__ break under this mode.

followUps.question: "So annotations validate my API inputs?"
followUps.html: Only because FastAPI and Pydantic read them and validate. A plain function or a dataclass accepts anything. If validation matters, it has to come from a library at the boundary.

followUps.question: What does typing.cast do at runtime?
followUps.html: Nothing: it returns its argument unchanged. It only tells the type checker to trust you. Same for TYPE_CHECKING blocks: they're False at runtime and exist to avoid import cycles.

followUps.question: How do you turn a Python function into an LLM tool definition?
followUps.html: Describe the arguments as a Pydantic model (or read the signature with inspect.signature + get_type_hints), call model_json_schema(), and send that as the tool's parameters. When the model calls the tool, validate its arguments with Model.model_validate_json() before running anything. The hint is the single source of truth for both schema and validation.

followUps.question: Would you enforce types at runtime everywhere, e.g. with typeguard or beartype?
followUps.html: Not everywhere. Validate at trust boundaries (requests, model output, queue messages) with Pydantic, and rely on static checking inside. Runtime checkers on every call add overhead and mostly duplicate what the static checker already proved. beartype in tests is a reasonable middle ground.

dontSay: "Python checks the annotations when you call the function."
"Hints slow down my code." — evaluating them costs almost nothing, and nothing per call.

python-q7.testing: whether you understand cooperative scheduling well enough to predict when concurrency happens and when it doesn't.
python-q7.trap: "async runs things in the background" or "on another thread."
python-q7.spoken:
"An async def function returns a coroutine object: a function that can pause and resume, keeping its frame. It doesn't run until something drives it.

The driver is the event loop, running on a single thread. You wrap coroutines in Tasks, and the loop steps each Task forward. A Task runs until it hits an await on something that isn't ready, like a socket read. At that point the coroutine suspends, control goes back to the loop, and the loop registers interest in that socket with the OS selector: epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS. When the OS reports the socket ready, a Future completes and the loop schedules the Task to resume right where it paused.

So the key word is cooperative. There's no preemption. A coroutine keeps the thread until it awaits. That's why you get thousands of concurrent network calls on one thread, and also why one CPU loop or one blocking call freezes every other request on that loop.

And concurrency isn't parallelism here: one core, interleaved waits. Also, await on a coroutine doesn't create concurrency by itself; it just runs it inline. You only get overlap when you create Tasks, with gather, a TaskGroup or create_task."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"A coroutine is a function that can pause at await; the event loop decides who runs next, and only at those pauses."

  • async def → calling it creates a coroutine object (a warning appears if it's never awaited).
  • Task = a coroutine scheduled on the loop. Future = a placeholder for a result that isn't ready yet.

stages.name: What the event loop does
stages.html:
• One loop iteration: run every callback in the ready queue → compute timeout until the next timer → select() for I/O → schedule callbacks for ready fds and expired timers.
  • A Task step is coro.send(None); the coroutine yields a Future up the await chain; the Task adds a done-callback to it that reschedules itself.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
import asyncio
async def worker(name, delay):
    print(name, "start")
    await asyncio.sleep(delay)
    print(name, "end")
async def main():
    await worker("A", 0.1)          # awaited inline: no overlap
    await asyncio.gather(worker("B", 0.2), worker("C", 0.1))
asyncio.run(main())
# → A start · A end · B start · C start · C end · B end   (one per line)

A runs alone because awaiting a coroutine directly just runs it. B and C are wrapped as Tasks by gather, so their waits overlap and C finishes first.

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints?  then in :
followUps.html: x then f. Calling f() only creates the coroutine; its body runs when it's awaited. If you never await it, Python warns "coroutine 'f' was never awaited" and f is never printed.

followUps.question: "So async runs my code in the background on another thread?"
followUps.html: No. Everything runs on the loop's one thread, interleaved at await points. Only to_thread/run_in_executor move work to other threads.

followUps.question: How does await asyncio.sleep(0) help?
followUps.html: It yields control to the loop once without waiting, letting other ready tasks run. It's a crude way to break up a long loop, but moving CPU work off the loop is the real fix.

followUps.question: Why must you keep a reference to a task from create_task?
followUps.html: The loop keeps only weak references to tasks. If nothing else holds the task, it can be garbage-collected mid-flight. Store it in a set and discard on completion, or use a TaskGroup, which owns its tasks.

followUps.question: How would you find what's blocking the loop in a live FastAPI service?
followUps.html: Watch event-loop lag as a metric (schedule a callback every second and measure how late it runs). When it spikes, py-spy dump --pid shows the frame on the loop thread. In staging, debug mode logs slow callbacks with their source. Then move the culprit to a thread or process.

followUps.question: How is Python's model different from Go's goroutines?
followUps.html: Goroutines are preemptively scheduled across many OS threads, and blocking calls don't block other goroutines. Python's asyncio is cooperative on one thread, with explicit await points, and a blocking call blocks everyone. The upside is no data races between awaits; the downside is every library must be async-aware.

python-q8.testing: whether you know the compact-dict layout and why ordering fell out of it.
python-q8.trap: "it's a hash table with a linked list for order," like Java's LinkedHashMap.
python-q8.spoken:
"Since CPython 3.6, a dict is two arrays. One is a sparse index table, sized as a power of two, holding small integers. The other is a dense array of entries, each storing the hash, the key and the value, in the order they were inserted.

To look up a key, CPython hashes it, uses the hash to pick a slot in the index table, and follows it to an entry. If the slot is taken by a different key, it probes to another slot using a perturbation of the hash, which is open addressing. It compares hashes first and only calls __eq__ when hashes match.

Ordering is a side effect of that layout: new entries are appended to the dense array, and iteration just walks that array. It started as a memory optimisation, about 20–25% smaller than the old layout, and 3.7 made insertion order a language guarantee.

When the table gets about two-thirds full, it resizes and rebuilds the index, but the dense order is kept. Deleting leaves a dummy marker. And keys must be hashable, with __hash__ and __eq__ agreeing, or lookups silently fail."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"A dict is a small sparse index pointing into a dense, append-only entries array. Order is structural, not bolted on."

indices:  [ -, 1, -, -, 0, -, 2, - ]        (1–8 bytes per slot)
entries:  [ (h1,'a',1), (h2,'b',2), (h3,'c',3) ]   ← insertion order

stages.name: What CPython does
stages.html:
• slot = hash & (size - 1); on collision, probe with perturb >>= 5; slot = (5*slot + 1 + perturb) & mask.
  • Compare cached hash first, then identity, then __eq__.
  • Resize when usable space runs out (load factor ~2/3); the index is rebuilt, dense order kept.
  • Delete marks the index slot as DUMMY and blanks the entry; holes are compacted on resize.
  • Key-sharing dicts (PEP 412): instances of the same class share one keys table, saving memory per object.
  • Language guarantee (3.7+): iteration follows insertion order. The layout itself is a CPython detail.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.claim: order kept, and the hash/eq contract
stages.html:
d = {"b": 1, "a": 2}; d["c"] = 3; del d["b"]; d["b"] = 4
print(list(d))
class Bad:
    def __init__(self, v): self.v = v
    def __eq__(self, o): return self.v == o.v
    __hash__ = object.__hash__           # identity hash: breaks the contract
print({Bad(1): "x"}.get(Bad(1)))
# → ['a', 'c', 'b']
# → None

Re-inserting b after deletion puts it at the end. The Bad keys are equal but hash differently, so the lookup misses.

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints?
followUps.html: {1: 'c'}. 1, 1.0 and True are equal and hash the same, so they're one key. The first key object inserted (1) is kept, and the value is overwritten by each later assignment.

followUps.question: "Dicts are ordered by key, right?"
followUps.html: No, by insertion order. sorted(d) gives key order. Also, OrderedDict still differs: its equality is order-sensitive and it has move_to_end, which is why it's used for LRU caches.

followUps.question: Why is dict lookup O(1) on average, and when isn't it?
followUps.html: Hashing picks a slot directly; with a low load factor, probe chains are short. Worst case is O(n) when many keys collide, e.g. a bad custom __hash__ returning a constant. That's also why string hashes are randomised.

followUps.question: Why are sets not ordered even though dicts are?
followUps.html: Sets use the older single-table layout optimised for membership tests, without the dense entries array. Their iteration order depends on hashes and history. Use dict.fromkeys(items) for an ordered de-duplication.

followUps.question: You're holding 10 million small records as dicts in a worker. What do you change?
followUps.html: Measure with tracemalloc first. Then: __slots__ classes or named tuples cut the per-object dict; better still, columnar storage (NumPy/Arrow/pandas) with one array per field, which also enables vectorised work. For lookups, keep one dict from ID to row index rather than a dict per record.

dontSay: "Dict ordering is a CPython implementation detail." — it's guaranteed since 3.7.
"It uses a linked list to keep order."

python-q9.testing: refcounting as the main engine, the cycle collector as the backstop, and why RSS doesn't drop.
python-q9.trap: "Python has a garbage collector" as the whole answer.
python-q9.spoken:
"In CPython, the main mechanism is reference counting. Every object has a count of references to it. When a name is rebound, a container drops it, or a function returns, the count goes down, and when it hits zero the object is freed immediately. That's deterministic: a file closes the moment its last reference goes away.

Reference counting can't free cycles, like two objects pointing at each other, or an object whose __dict__ refers back to itself. For those there's a cyclic garbage collector. It only tracks container objects, splits them into generations, and periodically finds groups that are only reachable from each other, then frees them. Young objects are checked most often because most die young.

Two things people get wrong. First, freeing an object doesn't mean returning memory to the OS. Small objects live in pymalloc arenas, and an arena is only released when every object in it is freed, so RSS often stays high after a big load. Second, the GC is tunable: gc.freeze() before forking workers avoids copy-on-write, and some services raise thresholds for fewer pauses.

This is all CPython. PyPy uses a tracing GC, so __del__ timing is not guaranteed there."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html:
"Reference counting frees almost everything, immediately. The cyclic GC is a backstop for reference cycles."

  • CPython detail: refcounting and the generational GC. The language only promises that unreachable objects may be reclaimed.

stages.name: What CPython does
stages.html:
Layer What it does When
Refcount ob_refcnt in every object header; free at zero immediately
Cyclic GC finds unreachable cycles among container objects when allocations minus deallocations pass a threshold
Allocator pymalloc: pools in arenas (16 KB pools, 1 MB arenas on 64-bit 3.10+) for objects ≤ 512 bytes; larger go to malloc arena freed only when fully empty
  • GC generations: 0, 1, 2 with thresholds gc.get_threshold(); survivors are promoted.
  • Objects with __del__ in cycles are collectable since 3.4 (PEP 442).

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
import gc, weakref
class Node: pass
a = Node(); r = weakref.ref(a)
del a
print(r() is None)                 # freed at once by refcount
gc.disable()
b = Node(); b.self = b; r = weakref.ref(b)
del b
print(r() is None, gc.collect() > 0, r() is None)
# → True
# → False True True

The self-referencing node survives del until the cycle collector runs.

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints?
followUps.html: 2: one reference from x, one from the temporary argument passed to getrefcount. It's a CPython detail and may differ in the free-threaded build.

followUps.question: "Python has a garbage collector, so I don't need to think about memory."
followUps.html: The GC only handles cycles. Anything still referenced — an unbounded cache, a module-level list, a closure — is never freed. Most production "leaks" are live references, not GC failures.

followUps.question: Why doesn't RSS drop after del big_list?
followUps.html: The list's pointer array (large) goes back via free, but millions of small int or str objects sit in pymalloc arenas. An arena is released only when it's completely empty, and survivors scattered across arenas pin them. glibc's malloc may also keep freed pages. Run the job in a subprocess or recycle workers (max_requests) if it matters.

followUps.question: Would you ever call gc.disable()?
followUps.html: In short-lived batch jobs or after gc.freeze() in pre-fork servers, yes, carefully: without cycles, refcounting frees everything anyway. In a long-running service, only if you've verified cycles aren't piling up, e.g. by watching gc.get_count() and memory over time.

followUps.question: What does __del__ guarantee?
followUps.html: Very little. In CPython it runs when the refcount hits zero or the GC collects the cycle, but not necessarily at interpreter exit, and on PyPy it runs whenever the GC gets to it. Use context managers or weakref.finalize for cleanup that matters.

dontSay: "del frees the object." — it removes one reference.
"Memory not returning to the OS means a leak."

python-q10.testing: the precedence of data descriptors, the instance dict, non-data descriptors and __getattr__.
python-q10.spoken:
"obj.attr calls type(obj).__getattribute__, which for normal objects is object.__getattribute__, and it follows a fixed order.

First it looks up attr on the type, walking the MRO. If it finds a data descriptor — something with __get__ and __set__ or __delete__, like a property — that wins, even over the instance dict.

Otherwise it checks the instance __dict__. If the name is there, that's the answer.

If not, it goes back to what it found on the type: if it's a non-data descriptor, like a plain function, it calls its __get__, which is how methods get bound to self. If it's an ordinary class attribute, it returns it as is.

If all of that fails, it raises AttributeError, and only then is __getattr__ called as a fallback.

The reason it matters: property, classmethod, staticmethod, __slots__ and bound methods are all descriptors. And __getattr__ versus __getattribute__ is a real performance and correctness difference: one is a fallback, the other intercepts everything."

stages.name: The one-line claim
stages.html: "Data descriptor on the type → instance __dict__ → non-data descriptor or class attribute → __getattr__."

stages.name: What CPython does
stages.html:
• MRO comes from C3 linearisation: Class.__mro__.
  • CPython caches type lookups (the type attribute cache, and 3.11+ specialised bytecode like LOAD_ATTR_INSTANCE_VALUE), so the common path is fast.

stages.name: Prove it
stages.html:
class A:
    @property
    def x(self): return "property"
    def m(self): return "method"
a = A()
a.__dict__["x"] = "dict"; a.__dict__["m"] = "dict"
print(a.x, a.m)
print(A.m.__get__(a, A))
# → property dict
# → <bound method A.m of <__main__.A object at 0x…>>

property is a data descriptor, so it wins over the dict. A function is non-data, so the instance dict shadows it.

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints?  then
followUps.html: 1. Assigning c.x = 2 creates an instance attribute that shadows the class one; deleting it removes only the instance entry, so lookup falls back to the class attribute.

followUps.question: "The instance dict is always checked first."
followUps.html: Not for data descriptors. A property on the class wins even if the instance dict has the same key. That's what makes read-only properties possible.

followUps.question: How does self get passed to methods?
followUps.html: Functions are non-data descriptors. obj.method calls function.__get__(obj, type), which returns a bound method object holding obj and the function. Calling it prepends obj as the first argument.

followUps.question: __getattr__ vs __getattribute__ — which would you implement for a lazy-loading proxy?
followUps.html: __getattr__: it's only called on a miss, so normal attributes stay fast, and you avoid recursion traps. __getattribute__ is for rare cases where every access must be intercepted.

followUps.question: Where has attribute lookup hurt you in a service?
followUps.html: Typical case: SQLAlchemy relationships are descriptors that lazy-load on access. Under async, touching user.orders outside an awaited load raises MissingGreenlet or triggers N+1 queries. The fix is eager loading (selectinload) so the descriptor finds data already present.

dontSay: "Python looks in the instance dict, then the class" (full stop).
"__getattr__ is called on every attribute access."

python-q11.testing: closures, functools.wraps, and whether you handle async functions and exceptions.
python-q11.trap: a wrapper that loses the signature, or times an async function's coroutine creation instead of its execution.
python-q11.spoken:
"A decorator is a function that takes a function and returns a replacement. For timing, the replacement records time.perf_counter() before and after calling the original, in a try/finally so failures are timed too, and passes *args, **kwargs straight through.

Three things break if you're careless.

First, metadata. Without functools.wraps, the wrapper's name, docstring, __module__ and, importantly, the signature and annotations are lost. FastAPI and Pydantic read the signature to build request parsing and schemas, so an unwrapped endpoint suddenly takes *args, **kwargs. wraps copies the metadata and sets __wrapped__ so inspect.signature sees the original.

Second, async functions. Calling an async def returns a coroutine immediately, so a sync wrapper measures microseconds and returns an un-awaited coroutine. I check inspect.iscoroutinefunction and return an async wrapper that awaits.

Third, where the output goes: I emit to a metrics histogram or a structured log with the function name, not print, and I don't let the timing code throw.

Stacking order matters too: decorators apply bottom-up, so the timer should usually be outermost."

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html:
• Same signature and metadata as the original (frameworks introspect it).
  • Works for sync and async functions.
  • Times failures too, and re-raises unchanged.
  • Negligible overhead; never breaks the call if the metrics backend fails.

stages.name: Runtime model
stages.html:
• @timed runs once at definition: f = timed(f). The wrapper closes over fn via a cell (wrapper.__closure__).
  • Decorators with arguments (@timed(name="x")) are a factory returning the decorator: three levels.

💻 Prove it — sync and async in one decorator:

import asyncio, functools, inspect, time
def timed(fn):
    if inspect.iscoroutinefunction(fn):
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        async def aw(*a, **k):
            t = time.perf_counter()
            try: return await fn(*a, **k)
            finally: print(fn.__name__, f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")
        return aw
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def w(*a, **k):
        t = time.perf_counter()
        try: return fn(*a, **k)
        finally: print(fn.__name__, f"{time.perf_counter() - t:.2f}s")
    return w
@timed
async def fetch(): await asyncio.sleep(0.2)
asyncio.run(fetch())
# → fetch 0.20s

stages.name: The hard part
stages.html:
import functools, inspect
def bare(fn):
    def w(*a, **k): return fn(*a, **k)
    return w
def good(fn):
    @functools.wraps(fn)
    def w(*a, **k): return fn(*a, **k)
    return w
def f(q: str, limit: int = 10): ...
print(inspect.signature(bare(f)), inspect.signature(good(f)))
# → (*a, **k) (q: str, limit: int = 10)

FastAPI uses exactly this signature to decide query parameters and validation.

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints? Decorators  above  on , where each prints its name when applied.
followUps.html: b then a. Decoration applies bottom-up: f = a(b(f)). At call time, a's wrapper runs first (outermost), then b's.

followUps.question: "functools.wraps is cosmetic, it just fixes the name."
followUps.html: It also copies __doc__, __module__, __qualname__, __dict__ and sets __wrapped__, which inspect.signature follows. Frameworks that introspect signatures (FastAPI, Typer, Pydantic's validate_call, pytest fixtures) depend on it.

followUps.question: How do you write a decorator that takes arguments?
followUps.html: A factory: def timed(name): def deco(fn): @wraps(fn) def w(...): ...; return w; return deco. Supporting both @timed and @timed(name=...) needs a check on whether the first argument is callable.

followUps.question: Would you write this decorator or use something existing?
followUps.html: In a service, I'd use OpenTelemetry instrumentation (tracer.start_as_current_span as a decorator) or the metrics library's timer, so timings land in the same traces and dashboards as everything else. A hand-written one is fine for a script or as an interview demonstration.

followUps.question: What does a decorator cost per call?
followUps.html: One extra Python frame plus the timing calls, well under a microsecond on modern CPython. It matters only on very hot tiny functions; don't time those individually, profile them instead.

dontSay: "One sync wrapper works for async functions too."

spine: What I'd pick for an AI backend
python-q12.testing: the __enter__/__exit__ protocol, exception handling in __exit__, and composition with ExitStack.
python-q12.trap: "it's just syntactic sugar," or accidentally suppressing exceptions.
python-q12.spoken:
"Semantically, a with block is a try/finally: __enter__ acquires, __exit__ is guaranteed to run. The difference is where the cleanup logic lives. With try/finally, every call site has to remember the right cleanup, in the right order. With a context manager, cleanup travels with the resource: the author writes it once, and every caller gets it right by default.

__exit__ also receives the exception type, value and traceback, so it can react: roll back a transaction on error, commit on success. If it returns a truthy value, it suppresses the exception, which is powerful and a classic bug when done by accident.

They compose. Several resources in one with unwind in reverse order, and ExitStack or AsyncExitStack handle a dynamic number of resources. contextlib.contextmanager turns a generator into one, with the yield as the body.

In an AI backend they're everywhere: DB sessions and transactions, HTTP clients, tracing spans, temp files, locks and semaphores, and FastAPI's lifespan, which loads the model at startup and releases it at shutdown."

stages.name: Frame the axis
stages.html:
"Both guarantee cleanup; a context manager moves the cleanup from every caller to the resource."

mgr = open(path)            # what `with open(path) as f:` does, roughly
f = mgr.__enter__()
try:
    ...                     # body
except BaseException as e:
    if not mgr.__exit__(type(e), e, e.__traceback__): raise
else:
    mgr.__exit__(None, None, None)

stages.name: Where context managers win
stages.html:
💻 Prove it — commit on success, roll back on error, never swallow:

from contextlib import contextmanager
@contextmanager
def transaction(log):
    log.append("begin")
    try:
        yield
        log.append("commit")
    except Exception:
        log.append("rollback"); raise
log = []
try:
    with transaction(log): raise ValueError("bad row")
except ValueError: pass
print(log)
# → ['begin', 'rollback']
  • ExitStack: open N files or N clients determined at runtime, all closed in reverse on exit.
  • contextlib.suppress(FileNotFoundError), closing(), nullcontext() (for an optional lock).

stages.name: The deciding question
stages.claim: will anyone else acquire this resource?
stages.html:
• If yes, give it a context manager so the cleanup can't be forgotten.
  • Watch the suppression rule: a __exit__ that ends with return True, or a @contextmanager that catches without re-raising, swallows errors silently.

stages.name: What I'd pick for an AI backend
stages.html:
Resource Context manager

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints? A context manager whose  returns ; inside it ; after the block .
followUps.html: after. The ZeroDivisionError is passed to __exit__, which returns a truthy value, so it's suppressed and execution continues after the with. Returning None (the default) would re-raise.

followUps.question: "Context managers are just syntactic sugar for try/finally."
followUps.html: The guarantee is the same, but the value is ownership and reuse: the cleanup is written once by the resource's author, can inspect the exception, can suppress it, and composes with ExitStack. That's more than sugar.

followUps.question: What if __enter__ raises?
followUps.html: __exit__ is not called: the resource was never acquired. So __enter__ must clean up any partial acquisition itself.

followUps.question: How does FastAPI's lifespan use this?
followUps.html: @asynccontextmanager async def lifespan(app): code before yield runs at startup (load the model, create the HTTP client and DB pool), code after runs at shutdown (close them). It replaces on_event hooks and guarantees cleanup order, which matters for GPU memory and open connections.

followUps.question: Why is a @contextmanager generator easy to get wrong?
followUps.html: Without a try/finally around yield, an exception in the body skips the cleanup after yield. And if you catch the exception without re-raising, it's suppressed. The pattern is try: yield; finally: cleanup().

dontSay: Creating an httpx.AsyncClient per request inside async with.

python-q13.testing: validation at the boundary, not everywhere; and concrete v2 knowledge.
python-q13.trap: Pydantic models used as domain objects and re-validated on every internal hop.
python-q13.spoken:
"Pydantic sits at the boundaries of the service, where untrusted data comes in or goes out: HTTP requests and responses, queue messages, config from the environment, and the outputs of LLMs and tools. Its job is to turn untrusted input into typed, validated objects once, at the edge, so the core can trust them.

It does three things from one class definition: validation with coercion, like the string '5' becoming an int in lax mode; serialisation with model_dump and model_dump_json; and JSON Schema generation. That last one matters in AI backends: the same model that validates a tool call's arguments generates the tool's schema for the LLM.

v2 changed a lot. The core, pydantic-core, is written in Rust, so validation is much faster — the maintainers cite roughly 5 to 50 times versus v1. The API was renamed: parse_obj became model_validate, .dict() became model_dump, @validator became @field_validator and @model_validator, and Config became model_config. There's a strict mode that turns off coercion, and TypeAdapter validates plain types without a model.

The main design rule: validate once at the edge, keep the core on dataclasses or plain objects, and map ValidationError to a structured 422, not a stringified 500."

stages.name: Constraints
stages.html:
• Inputs you don't control: clients, webhooks, queue payloads, env vars, LLM output.
  • Requirements: clear errors for callers, schemas for docs and tool definitions, cheap enough for hot paths.

stages.name: Where it sits
stages.html: • Settings: pydantic-settings BaseSettings validates env config at startup, so a bad value fails the deploy, not the 3 a.m. request.

stages.name: The hard part
stages.html:
💻 Prove it:

from pydantic import BaseModel, ValidationError, Field
class ToolArgs(BaseModel):
    query: str
    top_k: int = Field(5, ge=1, le=50)
print(ToolArgs.model_validate({"query": "gil", "top_k": "7"}))
try:
    ToolArgs.model_validate({"query": "gil", "top_k": 500})
except ValidationError as e:
    print(e.errors()[0]["type"], e.errors()[0]["loc"])
print(ToolArgs.model_json_schema()["properties"]["top_k"])
# → query='gil' top_k=7
# → less_than_equal ('top_k',)
# → {'default': 5, 'maximum': 50, 'minimum': 1, 'title': 'Top K', 'type': 'integer'}
  • Lax mode coerced "7" → 7. model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True) rejects it, which is what you want for internal contracts.
  • e.errors() is structured: location, type, message. Return it as a 422 body.

followUps.question: 🧪 What prints?  then
followUps.html: 1 3. Lax mode accepts True as an int (it is a bool subclass) and 3.0 because it has no fractional part. M(x=3.5) fails with int_from_float. In strict mode, both True and 3.0 are rejected.

followUps.question: "Pydantic validates types, so my data is correct."
followUps.html: It validates shape and constraints you declared. Business rules — does this customer own this order, is this date in the future — belong in the domain layer or explicit validators. Schema-valid isn't semantically valid.

followUps.question: Dataclass or Pydantic for internal objects?
followUps.html: Dataclasses (or attrs) for the core: no validation cost, no framework dependency. Pydantic at the edge. If you need validation on a dataclass-shaped type at a boundary, TypeAdapter(MyDataclass) or pydantic.dataclasses do it.

followUps.question: How do you migrate a large service from v1 to v2?
followUps.html: Run bump-pydantic for mechanical renames, use pydantic.v1 imports as a temporary shim for hard cases, and pin tests on serialised output, because defaults changed (e.g. v2 no longer coerces int to str, and Optional[X] fields without a default are now required). Migrate module by module behind a green test suite.

followUps.question: How does Pydantic fit an LLM tool-calling loop?
followUps.html: The tool's argument model generates the JSON Schema sent to the model; when the model calls the tool, model_validate_json checks the arguments; on failure, the structured errors go back to the model in a bounded repair loop. One class is the contract in both directions.

dontSay: "I validate at every layer to be safe."
"Pydantic v2 is a rewrite in Rust" — the core is Rust; the API is still Python.
